[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Demystifying Model Quantization in PyTorch: PTQ, QAT, and bitsandbytes"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Deep learning models are traditionally trained using 32-bit floating-point precision (FP32). While effective, FP32 models demand significant memory and computational resources. Model quantization reduces precision to lower-bit representations (such as INT8 or INT4), drastically decreasing memory footprints and accelerating inference with minimal loss in accuracy."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Understanding Post-Training Quantization (PTQ)"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) is applied after a model has already been fully trained. It converts the weights (and optionally activations) from FP32 to INT8. PTQ is fast and requires no retraining, making it ideal when computational budgets are limited."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"import torch
import torch.nn as nn

# Define a simple model
class SimpleModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc = nn.Linear(10, 2)
        
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.fc(x)

model = SimpleModel().eval()

# Apply dynamic quantization to Linear layers
quantized_model = torch.quantization.quantize_dynamic(
    model, 
    {nn.Linear}, 
    dtype=torch.qint8
)
print(quantized_model)"},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Quantization-Aware Training (QAT)"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) simulates quantization effects during the training or fine-tuning process. By inserting fake-quantization modules into the forward pass, the optimizer learns to adapt weight updates to the eventual quantization loss, yielding higher accuracy than PTQ."},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"model.train()
# Prepare the model for QAT by fusing modules and inserting observers
model.qconfig = torch.quantization.get_default_qat_qconfig("fbgemm")
prepared_model = torch.quantization.prepare_qat(model)

# Training loop would happen here...
# After training, convert to quantized equivalent
prepared_model.eval()
final_qat_model = torch.quantization.convert(prepared_model)"},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Ultra-Low Precision with bitsandbytes"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"For massive Large Language Models (LLMs), bitsandbytes enables 8-bit and 4-bit quantization (such as NF4 and FP4) directly inside PyTorch. This makes it possible to load billion-parameter models onto consumer-grade GPUs without crashing from out-of-memory errors."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig

    bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.float16,
